items.stem: A pharmacist receives a written Schedule II morphine prescription for an adult Massachusetts patient living in a licensed LONG-TERM CARE FACILITY. The original prescription is 15 days old, and the pharmacist confirms valid LTCF status and a continuing order for individual-unit partial dispensing. A different patient lives independently at a residential apartment complex that calls itself 'senior care,' but that residence is NOT a qualifying LTCF and the second patient has no documented terminal illness or other partial-fill basis. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Both patients automatically qualify for the 60-day LTCF partial-dispensing provision because they are older adults.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 21 CFR 1306.13(c) status exception requires an actual LTCF patient or medically documented terminal illness.

choices.text: The documented LTCF patient may use that unit-dose partial-fill pathway while the prescription is otherwise valid; the other patient does not qualify solely from the residence's marketing name.
choices.why: Correct. The federal status route is patient-specific and does not override Massachusetts Schedule II validity.

choices.text: Neither patient can receive any partial dispensing because Massachusetts prohibits dividing all Schedule II prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts and federal law provide permitted partial-dispensing pathways under specified conditions.

choices.text: The LTCF patient automatically may receive further partial dispensing 60 days after issue regardless of Massachusetts expiration.
choices.why: Incorrect. M.G.L. c.94C §23(a) makes a Massachusetts Schedule II prescription invalid after 30 days, despite the federal LTCF upper window.

items.novelty_note: Tests qualifying patient category and state 30-day overlay, rather than old question's expired 34th day.

items.stem: Pharmacy A in Massachusetts receives a patient's new EPCS Schedule II prescription, enters it into the computer, adjudicates an insurance claim and prints a pharmacy label. The prescription is never physically supplied to the patient. The pharmacy cancels the claim and returns the product to stock. The patient requests a transfer for INITIAL DISPENSING to Pharmacy B, which has compatible EPCS systems. A clerk argues that reversal of an insurance claim BY ITSELF proves the prescription is legally unfilled. What should the pharmacists do?

choices.text: Treat insurance reversal alone as dispositive and send the paper label by fax as an initial EPCS transfer.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1306.08(f) requires direct pharmacist electronic transfer without converting to fax; billing entries alone do not settle dispensing status.

choices.text: Verify and document whether any quantity was legally dispensed and whether the prescription remains eligible for initial dispensing; if so, use the one-time compliant electronic pharmacist-to-pharmacist transfer.
choices.why: Correct. The legal transfer condition is initial dispensing, with actual dispensing history and original electronic record integrity determining applicability.

choices.text: Refuse all transfers whenever an insurance claim was ever submitted, even if no medication was dispensed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule is based on initial dispensing and other legal conditions, not a categorical billing-claim bar.

choices.text: Send an email containing a scan of the original order because both pharmacies already know its drug and patient details.
choices.why: Incorrect. The controlled EPCS transfer must remain in the original electronic form without prohibited alteration.

items.novelty_note: Separates actual dispensing history from billing reversal or printed label; conditional final status requires audit.

items.stem: A patient received a TEN-DAY Schedule VI medication supply from a Massachusetts hospital pharmacy while being discharged after surgery, pursuant to its discharge-dispensing authority. The patient now goes to an unrelated retail pharmacy, asking for a 'refill' based only on the hospital's old dispensing label. The hospital discharge order included no separate valid retail prescription or refill authorization. What is the proper response?

choices.text: Dispense a new month under the hospital label because hospital discharge dispensing creates transferable retail refill authorization.
choices.why: Incorrect. A prior discharge dispensing transaction does not independently create a new outpatient prescription/refill at a retail pharmacy.

choices.text: Contact the authorized prescriber for a valid new prescription or other lawful continuing authorization before dispensing more; the old hospital label alone is insufficient.
choices.why: Correct. 105 CMR 722.090(B) treats the hospital discharge supply as limited and nonrefillable at the hospital; retail needs its own valid dispensing authority.

choices.text: The retail pharmacy must dispense exactly the remaining four days because the hospital could have dispensed fourteen days.
choices.why: Incorrect. The hospital's unused maximum supply capacity is not an unissued retail order transferable to another pharmacy.

choices.text: A pharmacy technician may simply alter the hospital label into a new prescription record without a prescriber.
choices.why: Incorrect. Data entry cannot create otherwise absent prescription authorization.

items.novelty_note: Retail follow-on without valid Rx after hospital discharge, separate from hospital's own 14-day limit.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy compounds a patient-specific NONSTERILE topical preparation with a supported assigned BUD of 21 days and a required refrigeration condition. The final prescription container has the ordinary patient, prescriber and drug identity information, but the proposed label shows only the raw ingredient's manufacturer expiration of 2028 and DOES NOT identify the product as compounded. Which changes are appropriate before dispensing? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Identify the medicine as a nonsterile compounded drug preparation on the container label.
choices.why: Correct. M.G.L. c.94C §21 explicitly requires compounded preparations to be identified as sterile or nonsterile.

choices.text: Use the ingredient's 2028 manufacturer expiry as the only date, even though a 21-day compounded BUD was assigned.
choices.why: Incorrect. A component expiration does not substitute for the preparation's justified beyond-use date.

choices.text: Label or otherwise supply the assigned 21-day BUD and required storage conditions as applicable to the compounded preparation.
choices.why: Correct. The compounded preparation's BUD and storage conditions must control use, not only the raw ingredient label.

choices.text: Remove the patient name entirely because patient-specific compounded products follow only the FDA manufacturer's original OTC label rules.
choices.why: Incorrect. These are patient-specific prescription compounded preparations subject to prescription labeling duties.

items.citation: M.G.L. c.94C §21 (compounded preparation labeling); 247 CMR 9.01(3); Board MOR Advisory compounded products
items.novelty_note: Compounded topical label, assigned BUD vs ingredient expiry, distinct from ordinary commercial Rx label.

items.stem: A Massachusetts licensed pharmacist uses MassPAT before dispensing a new opioid prescription. A technician whom the pharmacist specifically authorized as a MassPAT DELEGATE also needs to run a patient search. Another employee proposes borrowing the pharmacist's login credentials; a different technician wants to search a celebrity neighbor out of curiosity. Which actions are appropriate under MassPAT's published terms and registration guidance? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The authorized delegate registers and uses the delegate's own MassPAT account for a legitimate assigned patient-care search.
choices.why: Correct. MassPAT has a specific delegate registration process requiring an authorizing prescriber or pharmacist account.

choices.text: The technician may use the pharmacist's login and password, because both employees work at the same pharmacy.
choices.why: Incorrect. MassPAT terms prohibit sharing usernames, passwords and other access credentials.

choices.text: The pharmacist limits searches to authorized treatment/dispensing evaluations and protects access from unrelated personal curiosity.
choices.why: Correct. MassPAT access is for qualifying patient-care functions, not a general people-search database.

choices.text: A delegate may use the integrated hospital EHR access without a MassPAT delegate account whenever the pharmacist authorizes it verbally.
choices.why: Incorrect. MassPAT's current EHR integration page says delegates use the MassPAT web portal, not delegate-integrated EHR access.

items.citation: MA MassPAT Terms and Conditions §§1–4; MassPAT registration guide / EHR integration
items.novelty_note: Distinguishes individual credential security from valid delegated patient-care access.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist checks MassPAT before dispensing a patient's new controlled prescription. The query returns a recent opioid entry under a very similar name, but the date of birth and address do not match the patient in front of the pharmacist. The patient reports never filling that opioid. The pharmacy can verify patient identifiers and contact the record's dispenser. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Automatically classify the patient as opioid-shopping and reject the prescription because a similar name proves identity.
choices.why: Incorrect. MassPAT findings with conflicting key identifiers are not verified patient-specific evidence.

choices.text: Reconcile identity and record accuracy, assess the actual patient's medication history and prescriptive legitimacy, then exercise professional judgment.
choices.why: Correct. MassPAT assists prospective review but requires accurate attribution and contextual assessment.

choices.text: Erase the opioid claim directly from the state database using the pharmacist's password to speed up the decision.
choices.why: Incorrect. A dispensing pharmacist cannot arbitrarily delete another dispenser's reported transaction.

choices.text: Ignore MassPAT for all future prescriptions because one questionable match proves that the registry is unusable.
choices.why: Incorrect. A potentially incorrect match calls for verification rather than blanket abandonment of prospective review.

items.citation: 247 CMR 9.15(1)–(2), 9.17(1)–(2); MA MassPAT patient search guidance
items.novelty_note: Decision hinges on conflicting DOB/address and confirming records, not number of controlled dispensings.

items.stem: A retail business in Massachusetts plans to sell TEN-tablet packages of an FDA-regulated OTC acetaminophen product without any patient-specific prescription. It pours tablets from compliant manufacturer-labeled child-resistant bottles into transparent zipper bags marked only 'acetaminophen—10 tablets.' The new bags omit Drug Facts, dosage directions, warnings and suitable special packaging. Which is the best regulatory conclusion?

choices.text: The bags may be sold because a pharmacist need not provide prescription labels for OTC transactions.
choices.why: Incorrect. OTC nonprescription sales still require applicable FDA Drug Facts labeling and PPPA packaging compliance.

choices.text: Do not offer the unlabeled zipper bags for retail sale as described; lawful OTC repackaging must satisfy applicable product labeling and packaging requirements.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 201.66 requires Drug Facts on OTC retail labeling and 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(16) covers specified acetaminophen special packaging.

choices.text: Sell them if the cashier orally reads the manufacturer's original warning once to each purchaser.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verbal counseling does not replace required OTC package labels or special packaging.

choices.text: Treat the bags as valid Rx containers by printing a patient's name on each bag, despite no prescription being issued.
choices.why: Incorrect. An invented patient-specific label does not convert general OTC merchandise into a lawfully labeled prescription.

items.citation: 21 CFR 201.66; 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(16); FDA OTC Drug Facts and CPSC acetaminophen special-packaging rules
items.novelty_note: Distinguishes non-prescription merchandise repackaging from patient-specific Rx dispensing.
